title: Shridhar's feast and the all-night jagran
hookLine: a little girl tells a poor man to feed the whole village, and a Punjabi lane stays up all night for her
carry: the mother feeds everyone who comes
tomorrow: why throw sesame into a winter fire?

lines: A POOR MAN, A LITTLE GIRL.
cards: In the hills of Jammu, the story goes, lived a poor man named Shridhar who loved the Goddess. One day a little girl came to him and said: hold a feast, a bhandara, and invite the whole village.
Shridhar looked at his kitchen. He could barely feed himself. But he went door to door anyway, and the whole village came, far more people than his little house could hold.
Today, what the girl did next, and why a Punjabi family still stays up all night for her.

teach.b: As the shrine's legend tells it, the girl served everyone herself, and every guest ate. One guest, a proud yogi named Bhairon, demanded meat and wine, and when she refused, he tried to grab her.
She slipped away up the Trikuta mountain. Shridhar was heartbroken, until, the story says, she came to him in a dream and showed him her cave.
That cave is Vaishno Devi, one of India's most visited shrines, where pilgrims climb day and night calling Jai Mata Di: victory to the Mother. Here's the teaching inside the story.
In devotion to the Goddess, she is Mata, Mother: the one who feeds, and who comes in the smallest form, a little girl, to a man with nothing.
That's why at Navratri many families wash the feet of young girls and feed them as the Goddess.

teach.h: JAGRAN: A NIGHT AWAKE IN THANKS
teach.b: And it's why a Punjabi family whose prayer was answered, a baby born, an illness passed, holds a jagran: a waking, a vigil. A picture of the Mother goes up in a tent in the lane.
The lamp before her, the jyot, burns till dawn. Singers lead bhents, songs offered to her, and kids fall asleep on laps. At dawn comes prasad, food offered to her and then shared.
And the whole lane is invited, like Shridhar's village. You don't thank the Mother and keep the blessing to yourself. What she gives, you set before her, then share with everyone who comes.

how: Punjabi Hindu families hold a jagran, or jagrata, for Mata, often in thanks for a blessing: singers lead devotional songs through the night before a lit jyot, the neighbors are invited, and prasad is shared at dawn.

games.q: what does “punjab's shared devotional ground” mean?
o: a pilgrimage on foot to a shrine in the hills
a jagran, a night awake singing to the Mother in thanks
a fast kept in silence from sunrise until sunset

games.q: Shridhar's feast and the jagran — tap the pairs.
p: the poor man told to feed the village
the lamp kept burning all night

s: in the legend, Shridhar's feast ran out of food
the girl served everyone herself, and every guest ate.
a family may hold a jagran in thanks
for a birth, a wedding, a new house, an illness passed, a prayer answered.
the prasad at a jagran is kept for the family
it's shared at dawn with everyone who came, the whole lane.

games.q: your little brother's surgery went well, and your family wants to thank the Mother. by Shridhar's story, what fits?
o: a quiet prayer, and keep the news in the family.
a jagran: a night of songs for her, and the whole lane fed at dawn.
a big donation, so nobody has to come over.
games.why: the Mother feeds everyone, so her thank-you is shared: a night awake for her, and prasad for all who come, as Shridhar fed his village.

practice: Let the tent's words ride on your breath. If you pray, say Jai Mata Di softly on each out-breath, and on each in-breath bring to mind one thing that came to you this year as a gift.
If you don't pray, simply name the gifts, one per breath, and for each one, think of someone you could share it with.

wordCard.voice: Punjab's shared devotional ground. Today, the jagran: a night awake for the Mother, with the whole lane invited, the way Shridhar invited his village. Today's word.

orig.note: a waking or vigil: staying up through the night for God.

carryVoice: Your line: the mother feeds everyone who comes. A lamp kept lit, and a lane kept company, until dawn. Rest well.

sources.ref: Vaishno Devi shrine legend: Pandit Shridhar's bhandara, Bhairon Nath, the flight to Trikuta and the cave shown in a dream (shrine tradition)
the Punjabi jagran or jagrata for Mata: the jyot, bhents, prasad at dawn (living practice)
kanya puja (kanjak) at Navratri: young girls honored and fed as the Goddess (living practice)
